claim: Treat the first version of any design as disposable draft material — ship an intentionally rough pass, then improve it across further passes rather than trying to get it right in one attempt.
why: Quality is an emergent property of repeated attempts, not of care taken on a single attempt; holding a first draft to a final-quality bar stalls the process before iteration can do its work.
when: Any new design from a blank state, especially by someone still building their instincts.
fails: Contexts with a hard one-shot delivery — client-facing final handoff, a production launch, or a brief that requires a single polished artifact — where iterations must happen privately before the one visible version.

claim: Prioritise the number of designs completed over the polish of any single design; produce many finished-enough pieces instead of endlessly refining one.
why: Volume exposes you to more design problems and more of your own bad choices, which is what builds the judgement that makes later work good.
when: Skill-building phases and personal practice work where output count is under your control.
fails: Paid or portfolio work where a single sloppy artefact is the deliverable and quantity has no audience.

claim: When a design stops progressing, stop working on it — switch to a different piece of work and return to the stalled one in a later session.
why: Continued effort on a stuck design produces no forward movement; distance restores the fresh perspective needed to see the problem.
when: You've noticed you're rehashing the same decisions or feel stalled on a specific layout or composition.
fails: Deadline pressure makes abandonment costly, or the switching becomes avoidance and nothing ever gets finished.

claim: Never begin a design session by opening an empty canvas and waiting for an idea — go gather visual references or input first, then open the tool with something to react to.
why: A blank file gives you nothing to make decisions against; inspiration is an input you have to fetch, not something that arrives while you stare.
when: Starting fresh work, particularly early in your learning when you have little internalised visual vocabulary.
fails: Reference-gathering itself becomes the procrastination, or references are copied wholesale rather than used as a starting stimulus.

claim: Separate 'this design is bad' from 'I am bad at design' — read a weak first draft as a normal stage of the process rather than as a verdict on your ability.
why: Experienced designers also fail on first attempts, so a bad first pass carries no information about skill level and shouldn't trigger abandonment of the craft.
when: Evaluating your own early-stage output, especially when comparing it to finished work by others.

claim: Default to restrained execution — solid layout, type, contrast and hierarchy with minimal motion — and treat 3D, scroll-driven scenes and heavy animation as opt-in features that must be justified per project.
why: Elaborate effects consume large amounts of build time and client-side rendering budget while contributing nothing to whether the page communicates or converts; most site goals are met without them.
when: Standard product, SaaS, service and marketing sites whose success is measured in comprehension and conversion.
fails: Brand, campaign or portfolio work where the experience itself is the product and being remembered is the actual KPI.

claim: Before adding an effect, name the page's primary goal — conversion or awareness — and only spend heavily on spectacle when the goal is awareness/memorability.
why: A conversion page needs the fastest, clearest path to a purchase or signup; a brand page has no transaction to protect, so it can trade speed and simplicity for impression.
when: Deciding the ambition level of animation and interaction at the start of a project.
fails: Pages that carry both jobs — a brand-heavy landing page that still owns the signup — where spectacle must not sit between the user and the primary action.

claim: Kill any effect that measurably slows page load or makes navigation harder, regardless of how impressive it looks.
why: Usability is the base requirement; an effect that damages it has a negative net value even if it is beautiful.
when: Reviewing animations, WebGL scenes, transitions and scroll hijacking before shipping.

claim: Keep the user's location in the site legible at all times — persistent nav, visible current-page state, predictable page structure — and treat losing that as a failure even in an otherwise attractive design.
why: Knowing where you are is what lets someone navigate confidently; the chapter cites this as a specific reason a restrained design was judged great.
when: Multi-page products and marketing sites with more than a few destinations.

claim: Get visual interest from cheap, robust devices — a considered dark theme, subtle translucency/blur layers, restrained depth and light micro-motion — before reaching for 3D or physics.
why: These read as current and polished, cost almost nothing in performance, and degrade gracefully across screen sizes.
when: You want the work to feel contemporary without a large build budget.
fails: Overused translucency reduces text contrast and legibility; it needs sufficient backdrop contrast to stay accessible.

claim: Hold a design to three simultaneous tests — is it aesthetic, is it persuasive, is it usable — and treat passing all three as the definition of done rather than visual novelty.
why: The chapter judges the restrained examples 'effective' on exactly these grounds, which separates effectiveness from spectacle.
when: Critiquing or self-reviewing a finished layout.

claim: Where motion is used on a conversion site, keep it to a few small moving parts that support the message instead of a continuous animated narrative.
why: A limited amount of motion still conveys craft and draws attention to key points without the cost or navigational disruption of a full animated experience.
when: You want the site to feel alive but the primary job is still explaining and selling.

claim: Verify every layout across the full range of screen sizes as part of the base deliverable, not as a polish step — responsiveness is cited as a reason a design counts as good.
why: A design that only holds at one viewport isn't usable for most of its audience.
when: All web work.

claim: Don't use your ability to produce elaborate effects as the measure of your skill; judge yourself on whether the solution fits the brief's purpose.
why: Award-site aesthetics create a false benchmark; restraint is a deliberate, learnable judgement rather than a lack of ability.
when: Self-assessment, portfolio decisions, and choosing what to learn next.

claim: Before opening a design tool, spend a dedicated block of time collecting references and assembling a mood board; treat that as a required phase, not optional warm-up.
why: A design session started from a fragment of an idea runs out of direction partway through, and stalling mid-file tends to end in abandonment rather than recovery.
when: Starting a new site or page where the visual direction hasn't been established yet.
fails: Working inside an existing design system or brand where direction is already fixed, or on small iterative changes — the research phase becomes procrastination with no new decisions to inform.

claim: Don't commit to the first direction that excites you — collect several candidate directions and compare them before choosing one to build.
why: Enthusiasm for an early find crowds out alternatives you'd only discover by continuing to look, and those unfound alternatives are often better than the first hit.
when: The concept phase, when direction is still open and cheap to change.
fails: Under a hard deadline, or when exploration turns into indefinite collecting; at some point a good-enough direction chosen and executed beats a perfect one still being searched for.

claim: Treat 'I'm stuck and frustrated in the file' as a signal that the concept was underspecified, not that your execution skills failed — go back to references rather than pushing harder in the canvas.
why: The blocker is missing decisions upstream; more time in the tool cannot supply information that was never gathered.
when: Mid-project stalls where you can't decide what comes next on the page.
fails: The block is genuinely a craft problem — a spacing or type decision you can resolve in place — where retreating to research is avoidance.

claim: Use curated design galleries (Dribbble, Behance and equivalents) as deliberate idea sources during the research phase, and expect them to surface directions you would not have generated alone.
why: Your unaided pool of ideas is limited to what you already know; external reference expands the option set before you commit.
when: Gathering inspiration for a new project's visual direction.
fails: Copying a single gallery result wholesale instead of using many references to inform an original direction, or letting trend-driven gallery work override the project's actual content needs.

claim: Define the concept to the point where you can describe the whole page — not just one section — before you start building it.
why: The narrated failure was having 'a sliver' of an idea, which carried the work only as far as that sliver reached.
when: Transitioning from research into layout work.

claim: Before producing any design work, spend deliberate time reverse-engineering finished interfaces: name the zones, trace the reading order, and measure the actual gaps and sizes rather than describing them impressionistically.
why: Design skill is largely pattern recognition; you cannot reproduce decisions you have never consciously noticed, and measuring forces the vague impression 'this looks clean' into a repeatable specification.
when: Early skill-building, or whenever you need to raise the ceiling on your own visual judgement rather than ship a specific screen.
fails: It substitutes for practice indefinitely — analysis alone never builds execution speed, and copying measurements without understanding the intent produces pastiche.

claim: Encode grouping in a hero text block with a stepped spacing scale rather than uniform gaps: keep the most-related pair tightest (heading to subtext ~8px), the next relation looser (eyebrow above heading ~12px), and the action furthest (buttons ~32px below).
why: Proximity is read as relatedness, so the size of each gap tells the eye which elements belong together and in what order to process them; equal gaps flatten that into an undifferentiated stack.
when: Any stacked cluster of eyebrow, heading, supporting copy, and CTA — hero sections, cards, empty states.
fails: The exact pixel values are tied to this type scale and viewport; at larger display sizes or on mobile the ratios matter, not the literal 8/12/32.

claim: Cap hero copy hard — roughly seven words in the headline and about fourteen in the supporting line.
why: The hero has one job: land the message during the first glance, before the visitor decides whether to stay. Extra words dilute that and slow comprehension.
when: Above-the-fold marketing and landing page copy where attention is unearned.
fails: Documentation, editorial, or product surfaces where the reader is already committed and needs completeness over speed.

claim: Give a hero text block a deliberately restrained footprint — do not let it fill or dominate the canvas.
why: Negative space around a block is what makes it read as intentional and lets the eye settle on it; a block that spans everything reads as a wall of text with no focal hierarchy.
when: Hero and above-the-fold compositions with a supporting visual.

claim: Keep the navbar visually quiet and let exactly one element — the primary account or signup action — carry emphasis; everything else stays small and low-contrast.
why: The nav is a utility layer, not the message; competing emphasis there steals attention from the hero and blurs which action the page actually wants.
when: Marketing sites and product landing pages with a top navigation bar.
fails: Dense application shells or dashboards where navigation is the primary task surface and needs more weight.

claim: Lay out around the image's focal point: place text, nav, and controls above, below, or to one side so the region containing the subject stays completely unobstructed.
why: Overlapping the subject damages both the image and the readability of whatever sits on it; treating the focal area as a reserved zone lets both elements do their job at full strength.
when: Hero sections built on a photographic or rendered asset with an identifiable subject.
fails: Full-bleed compositions that intentionally overlay type on imagery — those need a scrim, gradient, or blur to buy back contrast instead.

claim: Select hero imagery with quiet, low-detail regions wherever text will sit; if a candidate image is visually busy behind the copy, reject the image rather than compensating with text effects.
why: Busy backgrounds destroy the contrast that text needs, and the page reads as chaotic; the fix belongs at asset selection, since a landing page largely stands or falls on the quality of its main visual.
when: Any composition where copy and imagery share space or sit adjacent.
fails: When you have no control over the asset — then a scrim or contained text panel is the fallback.

claim: Create hierarchy inside small text pairs with opacity or colour instead of size — hold both lines at the same size (e.g. 15px) and drop the secondary line to roughly 55% opacity.
why: Size changes at small scales quickly look accidental or break the grid; lowering contrast recedes the secondary line into the background while preserving alignment and rhythm.
when: Stat blocks, metric labels, captions, list metadata — dense pairs where the size range available is small.
fails: When the reduced-contrast text carries essential information or must meet accessibility contrast minimums; 55% on a light background can fall below WCAG thresholds.

claim: Treat the recurring landing-page skeleton — nav, hero text block, hero image, supporting stats strip — as a default starting structure, then vary the surface treatment rather than the underlying zones.
why: Pages that look wildly different to a casual viewer usually share the same zone arrangement and reading flow; the skeleton is what works, and originality lives in typography, colour, and imagery on top of it.
when: Composing a new marketing or product landing page from scratch.
fails: Products whose value is genuinely not communicated by a hero-plus-proof structure, or when every competitor already uses the identical skeleton and differentiation matters more than convention.

claim: When you cannot explain why a design choice works, test it by substitution: swap in a deliberately worse alternative and observe what breaks.
why: The failure case makes the invisible rule visible — the busy-background swap proves the original image was chosen for its empty regions, not just its subject.
when: Studying reference work, or defending a design decision to a stakeholder.

claim: Run every teardown against four named lenses — proximity, contrast, consistency, hierarchy — so the analysis produces transferable principles instead of one-off observations.
why: A fixed checklist turns scattered noticing into pattern recognition that carries to the next page you look at.
when: Deliberate practice sessions analysing existing interfaces.

claim: To build execution skill, rebuild an existing design as an exact replica rather than redesigning it — match the real values, not the general vibe.
why: A redesign lets you substitute your own preferences and skip anything you can't yet execute; an exact copy has a pass/fail standard, so it forces you to actually resolve every decision the original designer made.
when: Early practice when you can recognise good design but can't yet produce it.
fails: Copied work must not be shipped or presented as original client/portfolio work; and once you can already execute reliably, replication stops teaching and becomes busywork.

claim: When replicating, measure and record the specific numbers — gap between cards, nav bar height, button padding on each axis — instead of eyeballing proportions.
why: Named quantities are what transfer to your next project; a visual impression doesn't. Measuring is what converts looking into a reusable spacing and sizing vocabulary.
when: Doing replication practice, or reverse-engineering a reference during real work.
fails: Absolute pixel values are viewport- and scale-specific — capture the underlying rhythm (a spacing step, a ratio) rather than treating one screenshot's numbers as universal.

claim: Treat section layout as choosing from a short enumerated menu, not as open-ended invention: decide arrangement first, then text alignment, then visual treatment.
why: The space of layouts that actually work is small and repeats across the industry. Framing design as picking a branch from a known tree removes blank-canvas paralysis and makes the decision reviewable.
when: Laying out any standard page section — hero, features, pricing, testimonials.
fails: Work that must feel genuinely novel or brand-defining; the menu covers conventional cases and will produce conventional results.

claim: For a hero, pick one of: text left / image right (or mirrored), image full-bleed behind text, text stacked above image, or — rarely — text below image.
why: These are the arrangements that repeat across real sites; the rarer orderings are rare because they delay the message behind the visual.
when: Building a hero with both a headline and a supporting visual.
fails: Text-below-image inverts the reading priority, so reserve it for cases where the image itself is the message.

claim: Choose hero text alignment from three options: centered (the default), left-aligned, or headline left with body copy and CTA pushed to the right column.
why: Centering suits short declarative statements; left alignment suits longer copy that needs a consistent reading edge; the split treatment fills wide viewports without stretching one text block.
when: Setting the type block of a hero or any large statement section.
fails: Centered alignment degrades once copy runs past a couple of lines — ragged both edges makes it harder to read.

claim: Choose the hero visual from three treatments: an image with defined borders/containment, a full-width image bleeding into the background, or a rotating carousel of several images.
why: Containment reads as a discrete object or product shot; a bleed reads as environment and mood; a carousel is for when no single image can carry the message alone.
when: Selecting the imagery treatment for a hero or feature block.
fails: A carousel that auto-rotates costs the user control and buries later slides — only use it when the images are genuinely equivalent in importance.

claim: Resolve every layout fork by asking what the content is trying to do, and let the answer set hierarchy — not by asking which option looks nicer.
why: The options are all individually valid, so aesthetics can't break the tie. Content intent is the only criterion that produces a defensible, consistent answer.
when: Any point where multiple layouts are plausible for the same section.

claim: When a section's job is to land a single statement, center the text, increase the font size well above body scale, and surround it with generous empty space.
why: Size and isolation are what signal importance; a statement competing with neighbouring content reads as ordinary copy.
when: Manifesto lines, positioning statements, single-idea hero headlines.
fails: Applied to sections with multiple items or long copy, where the same treatment wastes space and flattens hierarchy.

claim: In a features section, demote the text: the visual carries the meaning and the copy exists only to label and support it.
why: Features are understood by seeing them; the text's job is captioning, so giving it statement-level scale misdirects attention away from the thing being shown.
when: Feature showcases, product tours, capability sections.
fails: Abstract or non-visual features (compliance, guarantees, policy) have no meaningful visual, so the text must lead.

claim: If a features set has more items than fit comfortably in a row, replace the horizontal row or scroller with a bento grid of mixed-size tiles.
why: Content that runs off the edge of the screen is content most users never see; a bento grid brings every item into the vertical scroll while still letting tile size express relative importance.
when: Six or more features, or any set where horizontal overflow would hide items.
fails: Small sets don't justify a bento grid, and it breaks down when every item is genuinely equal-weight — varied tile sizes then imply a hierarchy that isn't real.

claim: Keep a searchable library of curated real-world screenshots organised by section type, and consult a large sample of one section before designing it.
why: Pattern recognition needs volume — the finite option set only becomes visible after seeing how many teams converged on the same handful of solutions.
when: Stuck on a specific section, or starting a section type you haven't built before.
fails: Browsing references as a substitute for building; the chapter's own exercise is replication, not collection. (Note: presented as a paid sponsor placement.)

claim: Treat layout and visual style as two separate passes: lock the structural layout first, then apply a style layer (colour temperature, corner radius, imagery, control size, texture) that can be swapped without touching structure.
why: The demo changes a page's entire emotional register twice while the arrangement of elements stays identical, proving style is an independent variable from structure.
when: Any time you need a design to hit a specific tone, or need to explore multiple brand directions for the same product
fails: Some tones genuinely demand structural change — a dense data tool and a playful consumer onboarding are not the same layout wearing different paint

claim: Start a visual direction by writing down two or three adjectives for the target feeling, then translate each adjective into concrete parameter settings before you design anything.
why: The chapter treats 'friendly' and 'professional' as briefs that decompose into specific, checkable decisions, which makes the result arguable rather than a matter of taste.
when: Kicking off a visual pass, or defending a style choice in review
fails: Adjectives alone don't discriminate if you never fix what they mean in parameters — 'clean' and 'modern' map to almost anything

claim: For a friendly, welcoming tone: use a warm background hue, saturated and illustrative imagery, generous corner radii, and oversized rounded buttons.
why: Warmth, roundness, and scale read as approachable and low-stakes.
when: Consumer products, onboarding, anything where you need to lower the user's guard
fails: Contexts where users need to trust the product with money, data, or risk — bubbly styling reads as unserious there

claim: For a modern, premium tone: pull corner radii down toward square, replace colourful imagery with restrained low-saturation photography, and add a subtle noise or grain texture to flat backgrounds.
why: Reduced radius and reduced colour read as restraint; a faint texture keeps a dark or flat surface from looking cheap and empty.
when: B2B tools, premium or enterprise-positioned products, anything that needs to signal seriousness
fails: Pushed too far it becomes cold and unwelcoming; noise applied heavily or over text hurts legibility and inflates asset weight

claim: Change imagery, not just colour tokens, when shifting tone — photography and illustration style carry more of the felt impression than the palette does.
why: In the re-skin, the visuals are called out as the element that changes 'substantially', doing the heaviest lifting in the mood shift.
when: Rebranding, tone shifts, or when a colour-only retheme still feels like the old design

claim: Design multi-step flows as a diagram of screens and transitions before designing any individual screen.
why: The chapter demonstrates the flow at the level of steps and branches, showing that the sequencing questions are answerable — and worth answering — before pixel decisions exist.
when: Onboarding, checkout, signup, account setup, or any task spanning more than two screens
fails: Single-screen or purely presentational work, where there is no sequence to reason about

claim: Put an escape hatch on any entry screen a user can land on by mistake — for a signup form, a visible link to log in.
why: A meaningful share of arrivals at a signup page are existing users who took the wrong door; without an exit they either abandon or create a duplicate account.
when: Signup, account creation, or any flow with a sibling flow users routinely confuse it with

claim: When adding email verification, explicitly choose between hard-gating the flow on the code and soft-prompting while letting the user continue — and decide it against your product's risk, not by default.
why: The chapter presents both as legitimate: gating protects data integrity, soft-prompting protects completion rate; neither is universally correct.
when: Any verification, KYC, or confirmation step inside a conversion flow
fails: Soft-prompting fails where unverified accounts create real harm (billing, shared workspaces, abuse vectors); hard-gating fails where email delivery is slow or unreliable

claim: Ask segmenting questions (team size, role, use case) early enough in the flow that their answers can branch the remaining steps.
why: A question only earns its place if the flow behaves differently afterwards; asked too late, it is friction that changes nothing.
when: Onboarding flows that serve materially different user types
fails: When you have no branch to feed — collecting the answer for analytics alone doesn't justify the extra step

claim: Skip steps entirely for users the step doesn't apply to rather than showing them a dismissible or empty version.
why: The individual path bypasses 'invite your team' outright, keeping the flow as short as that user's actual needs.
when: Branched flows where a step is meaningless for one segment
fails: Skipping a step users might later need can hide the feature — pair the skip with discoverable access afterwards

claim: Judge flow decisions against the user's journey — what they know, want, and can do at that moment — not against visual criteria like spacing or type.
why: The chapter closes by explicitly separating the two judgement domains, so critique aimed at the wrong one doesn't improve the flow.
when: Reviewing or critiquing a multi-step experience

claim: Do not build a public portfolio in your first months of learning design; spend that time on practice work and revisit the portfolio once your taste has stabilised.
why: Taste shifts quickly during early learning, so anything you publish now will read as dated to you within weeks and will be misrepresenting your actual level by the time anyone sees it.
when: You are a beginner in your first one to two months of deliberate design study and feel the pull to package what you have made.
fails: You need a portfolio on a hard deadline — a job application, a client pitch, a course requirement. Then ship the best version you can now and plan to replace it; a shipped imperfect portfolio beats an unshipped ideal one.

claim: Treat the size of the gap between your old and current work as your primary progress metric, not the quality of either piece in isolation.
why: A large delta proves your judgement moved; an absent delta means you have been repeating a style rather than developing one.
when: Reviewing your own archive, or deciding whether a period of practice actually taught you anything.
fails: Late in a career, where deliberate stylistic consistency is an asset and a large delta may signal drift rather than growth.

claim: Withhold 'wrong' as a verdict on earlier work; describe it in neutral, concrete terms (scale, motion volume, contrast) and let the comparison carry the judgement.
why: Labelling past work as bad teaches shame rather than discrimination; describing what changed teaches the learner what dimensions they can actually move.
when: Critiquing your own archive, or giving feedback on a beginner's early work.

claim: When refining a maximalist design, reduce along three specific axes: shrink oversized type toward a normal reading scale, cut the number of animated elements rather than just their duration, and reserve the remaining motion for elements that need attention.
why: Beginner maximalism is usually a volume problem, not a taste problem — every element competing at maximum intensity leaves no hierarchy, so selective reduction restores it.
when: A layout where headlines dominate the viewport and most elements have entrance or hover animation.
fails: Deliberately expressive or brand-forward work where in-your-face scale and motion are the point; restraint there just reads as generic.

claim: Default to animating a minority of elements on a page rather than all of them, and prefer small-amplitude movement over large.
why: Motion is a hierarchy signal — if everything moves, nothing is emphasised, and the page reads as noise.
when: Adding motion to a portfolio, marketing site, or any content-led interface.
fails: Showreels, award-site entries, or interactive experiments where the motion itself is the deliverable.

claim: Save dated versions of your own work rather than overwriting them, so you retain a before/after archive to measure taste against.
why: You cannot see your own progress without a preserved earlier reference point, and the comparison is the most convincing evidence of growth you will ever have.
when: Any ongoing personal site or long-running practice project.

claim: Before building anything, assemble a swipe file of roughly 20 sections of the specific type you intend to build (e.g. hero sections and feature sections), sourced from curated design galleries rather than random browsing.
why: You cannot design toward a standard you have never seen; a concentrated reference set calibrates your eye to what 'good' looks like in that exact component category, and gives you material to study and copy later.
when: Starting out in UI design, or entering an unfamiliar component/page type where you lack an internal quality bar.
fails: Collecting becomes the activity — an ever-growing board that is never annotated or rebuilt produces recognition without capability.

claim: Annotate your references instead of just saving them: mark up the spacing values, the hierarchy order, and which elements are visually grouped together.
why: Naming the underlying decisions converts a screenshot from something you like into a set of rules you can reapply; the three axes named are the ones that carry most of a layout's structure.
when: Any time you have collected reference work and want to extract transferable structure from it.
fails: Annotating everything you save — a couple of deeply marked-up references teach more than twenty shallow ones.

claim: Learn execution by cloning a design you admire exactly, pixel for pixel, rather than by making a loose 'inspired by' version.
why: Exact replication forces you to confront every decision the original designer made — spacing, type scale, alignment — including the ones you would have skipped or fudged if allowed to improvise.
when: The practice phase, once you have references and can read their structure; done as private skill-building work.
fails: Clones are presented as original work in a portfolio or shipped commercially — this is a training exercise, not a deliverable.

claim: Sequence your clone practice as: hero section, then the feature section from the same site, then a second site with a deliberately different layout.
why: Staying within one site first teaches internal consistency (how a system repeats itself), then switching to a structurally different site prevents you from memorising one layout as the only way to solve the problem.
when: Working through replication practice over roughly a week.
fails: The second site is stylistically similar to the first — the contrast in layout is the point, so pick something structurally unlike it.

claim: Restyle one layout you already built at least twice under opposing style briefs — for example warm and friendly versus modern and premium — while keeping the underlying structure fixed.
why: Holding layout constant isolates the styling variables (colour, type, radius, imagery, density), which is how you learn that visual tone is a controllable layer rather than something that comes bundled with a layout.
when: After you can execute a layout competently and want to develop range in visual direction.
fails: You also change the layout between versions — then you have made two different designs and learned nothing about styling as a variable.

claim: Practice UX by designing the exact screens where a user journey branches — take a flow with two user types and build the divergent screen for each (e.g. an invite-your-team screen for a manager, a solo setup screen for an individual).
why: Branch points are where product thinking actually happens: they force you to decide what each user type needs next, rather than styling a screen that any user could see.
when: Moving from visual UI practice into product/UX reasoning; onboarding flows are a good first case because the branching is explicit.
fails: You design both branches identically with only the copy swapped — the divergence in user goal should change the content and the primary action.

claim: Order your learning as perceive → replicate → vary → apply, and do not skip forward: study references before cloning, clone before restyling, restyle before designing original flows.
why: Each stage supplies the raw material for the next — you cannot vary a layout you cannot build, and you cannot build one whose structure you cannot read.
when: Structuring a self-directed design curriculum from a standing start.
fails: The learner already has one of the capabilities; the ordering is a dependency chain, not a mandatory time allocation.

claim: During the initial learning period, do not build a portfolio; spend the entire budget on producing skill, and treat presentation as a later, separate task.
why: Portfolio work optimises for how the output looks to an audience, which pulls effort toward polish and packaging before there is anything worth packaging.
when: The first month or so of deliberate practice, when most output is clones and exercises anyway.
fails: You are already job-hunting on a deadline, where some presentable work is a hard requirement.

claim: Bound your practice plan in explicit time — fixed-length stretches with a named deliverable each — rather than open-ended study.
why: A dated structure with concrete artefacts (20 references, 3 clones, 2 restyles, 2 screens) makes progress checkable and stops the learner from stalling in the comfortable input phase.
when: Self-directed learning without an instructor or external deadline.

claim: For product-led categories like skincare, default to a bright neutral background, generous white space, and large uncropped product photography before attempting anything unconventional.
why: The purchase decision rides on the product looking desirable; the page's job is to remove everything competing with it.
when: Designing landing or hero sections for physical consumer goods where visual appeal drives conversion.
fails: Brands whose positioning is deliberately maximalist, editorial, or countercultural, where category convention is the thing being subverted on purpose.

claim: Treat layout novelty as something to spend from a budget: introduce unusual structure where it serves content, and revert to convention everywhere else rather than making every element unusual at once.
why: The critique concedes that repetitive layouts are genuinely bad, yet the design fails because it applied novelty to every element simultaneously — the individual ideas aren't wrong, the accumulation is.
when: Any page where you want a distinctive visual identity but still need it to function.
fails: Pure showcase or portfolio work with no conversion goal, where the layout itself is the deliverable.

claim: Only give a persistent page-index or section-scroller navigation to pages long enough to need it; on a short marketing page it occupies prime screen real estate for no benefit.
why: Wayfinding affordances earn their space in proportion to how lost the user could get; a two-or-three-screen page never gets you lost.
when: Deciding whether to add side rails, section dots, or scroll indicators to a marketing site.
fails: Long-form documentation, one-page portfolios with many sections, or scroll-narrative pages where the index genuinely aids orientation.

claim: Keep social media links out of the top navigation on a commerce page; put them in the footer so the nav carries only paths toward purchase.
why: A social link is an exit from the funnel, so placing it beside primary navigation invites users to leave at the moment you most want them to stay.
when: Header navigation for e-commerce or product landing pages.
fails: Creator, artist, or community brands where the social presence is the product and following is the desired conversion.

claim: Let the hero product image run large and uninterrupted — avoid cutouts, notches, or decorative shapes that carve into the photograph.
why: Cropping shapes out of the image shrinks the product's visual footprint and pulls attention to the frame rather than the thing being sold.
when: Hero sections built around a single product shot.
fails: Deliberate collage or editorial layering where the cut is a consistent, repeated motif across the whole design.

claim: Represent social proof in the hero with a compact signal — a star rating, a review count, a recognisable customer logo — and save full written testimonials for a dedicated section further down.
why: The header has to communicate at a glance; a paragraph of quoted text demands reading time the visitor hasn't committed yet, while a rating conveys the same trust instantly.
when: Placing credibility signals above the fold.
fails: Landing pages built entirely around a single endorsement, where the quote is the headline.

claim: Test abstract decorative shapes against unintended readings before shipping them — if a silhouette resembles something unrelated and comical, it hijacks the design's tone.
why: Viewers pattern-match compulsively; once a shape reads as something else, that reading cannot be un-seen and undermines a premium positioning.
when: Adding abstract blobs, arcs, or geometric ornaments to a layout.
fails: Playful or child-oriented brands where an incidental cartoon reading is harmless or welcome.

claim: Sanity-check the actual numbers in placeholder copy — a free-shipping threshold, price, or discount must be plausible for the category, because implausible figures read as carelessness.
why: Filler content is still content; a shipping minimum far above the product's own price signals the designer never thought about the business.
when: Populating any UI with example data — pricing, thresholds, stats, dates.

claim: Critique a design element by element, naming what works before what doesn't, rather than rejecting the whole composition.
why: The teardown keeps the nav bar, the icon set, and the intent behind including social proof — separating good decisions from bad ones tells you what to preserve in the redesign and prevents throwing away the parts that were already solved.
when: Auditing an existing design before redesigning it.

claim: Secure the hero imagery before refining the layout — if no adequate product shot exists, create or render one, because the surrounding composition depends on it.
why: The redesign's core premise is that the product carries the page, so layout decisions made around a placeholder will be rebuilt once real imagery lands.
when: Redesigning product-led pages where the imagery is the primary visual weight.
fails: Data-dense or text-led interfaces where imagery is secondary and layout can be resolved independently.

claim: Before designing a screen type you haven't shipped before, collect a reference set of how established products solve it — capture the full flow, not just the hero screen — and design against that set rather than from imagination.
why: Patterns that already survived real users encode constraints (edge cases, empty states, error paths) you won't anticipate from a blank canvas; the segment's whole premise is that seeing how the best already solved a problem shortcuts your own thinking.
when: Starting an unfamiliar flow — onboarding, checkout, settings, paywall, search — or any pattern where convention carries user expectation.
fails: Reference-gathering substitutes for defining your own product's content and structure; the chapter itself cuts away to say structure has to come first, and copying surface patterns without that groundwork produces a coherent-looking but hollow interface.

claim: If your copy names a specific audience, every other layer — imagery, vocabulary, examples, iconography, colour — must visibly come from that audience's world; a stated niche with generic visuals reads as a lie.
why: Visitors verify claims against evidence on the page; when the design shows no knowledge of their trade, the promise of being 'built for you' has nothing backing it and trust does not form.
when: Marketing or landing pages for vertical software aimed at one occupation or industry.
fails: Horizontal, multi-audience products where over-specifying one vertical alienates the rest of the market — there, resonance has to come from job-to-be-done framing rather than industry props.

claim: Include at least one photographic or illustrative depiction of the real user in their real environment above or near the fold, rather than relying solely on type, UI screenshots, and abstract shapes.
why: People recognise themselves before they read; a picture of their context does identification work that body copy cannot, and its absence is what makes an otherwise clean page feel machine-made.
when: Product sites whose value depends on the visitor believing the tool understands their specific workflow.
fails: Contexts where stock-quality or off-domain imagery would be worse than none — a wrong or obviously generic photo damages credibility more than restraint does.

claim: Treat a page with no imagery of any kind as a defect to investigate, not a minimalist style choice.
why: Total absence of pictures is usually a symptom of building from a template or generator that defaults to text-and-boxes, and it produces a uniform, robotic texture across the whole page.
when: Auditing an existing site or reviewing generated output before shipping.
fails: Deliberately austere brands (developer tools, editorial, privacy-first products) where a text-only aesthetic is a considered position and is carried by exceptional typography and layout.

claim: Write one headline that states the concrete outcome the product delivers, and let it be the only promise in that slot — no stacked sub-claims competing for the same attention.
why: A single actionable promise tells the visitor within a second whether the product does their job; splitting the message across several hedged lines leaves them with nothing to act on.
when: Hero sections of product and SaaS landing pages.
fails: Products whose value genuinely requires demonstration rather than assertion, where the hero must lead with a live artefact or demo instead of a claim.

claim: When a site feels wrong but scores well on layout, spacing, and animation, redirect the fix upstream to research and positioning instead of adding visual sophistication.
why: Polish problems and resonance problems have different causes; restyling a page that lacks audience understanding just produces a more attractive version of the same emptiness.
when: Redesign requests framed as 'make it look more modern' or 'make it feel premium'.

claim: Diagnose a page by testing whether its stated audience could be swapped for any other without changing a single visual asset; if they could, the design carries no audience signal.
why: Interchangeability is the measurable form of soullessness — it proves the visuals were chosen independently of who the product serves.
when: Critiquing or reviewing an existing marketing page.

claim: Before redesigning, study two or three sites in the same category that already feel alive and isolate the specific device they share, rather than borrowing their surface aesthetics.
why: Sites that read as human tend to converge on the same underlying mechanisms; naming the mechanism gives you something transferable, while copying the look gives you nothing.
when: The research phase preceding a redesign.

claim: Before designing any page, assemble a reference collage: for each section of the page, pull the layout of a section you admire from a different existing site, stacking them top to bottom in the order your message should unfold.
why: It forces you to decide message sequence and page flow using concrete evidence rather than abstract intent, and it separates 'what goes where' from 'what it looks like'.
when: You have a defined brand direction or feeling but no page structure yet, and you need to move from mood to a buildable layout.

claim: Never copy a reference section unchanged — state at least one deliberate modification for each borrowed pattern (bigger imagery, less text, different alignment, different background treatment) tied to your own audience or message.
why: The reference solves someone else's problem; the modification is where your product's specifics enter the layout, and it keeps the result from reading as a clone.
when: Any time you lift a layout pattern from another site into your own wireframe.

claim: Treat the Frankenstein collage as disposable: once the section order is settled, delete all borrowed visual styling and keep only the boxes, hierarchy, and order as a wireframe.
why: The collage's styling comes from many incompatible design systems, so carrying it forward would produce an incoherent page; only the structural decision is worth keeping.
when: Transitioning from reference-gathering into actual design or build.
fails: If you skip this step and start styling directly on top of the collage, you inherit five conflicting type scales, colour systems and spacing rhythms.

claim: Zoom the whole page out to a single view before proceeding — visual incoherence between sections is only visible at page scale, not while working on one section at a time.
why: Section-by-section work hides the mismatch; the zoomed-out view is what exposes it.
when: After assembling or editing multiple page sections.

claim: Use hero background and section imagery to depict the customer's world rather than the product interface — show the objects and context of the people who would use the software.
why: Contextual imagery answers 'is this for me?' faster than a UI screenshot or generic abstract art.
when: Marketing pages for vertical or industry-specific software where the audience is narrow.

claim: Order a marketing landing page as: hero → logo ribbon → how it works → features → testimonials → CTA → footer.
why: It moves from who this is for, to proof it's used, to how it works, to what it does, to what others say, to the ask — each section earning the next.
when: Standard SaaS or product marketing pages with a single conversion goal.

claim: Don't rely on a logo ribbon alone for credibility — pair it with a testimonial section, since logos and quotes prove different things.
why: Logos show adoption; testimonials show experience. One without the other leaves an obvious gap.
when: Any page where you have both customer logos and quotable feedback.

claim: When adapting a feature section from a reference, enlarge the visual and cut copy aggressively — aim to remove the large majority of the reference's text.
why: Reference sites over-explain; the image carries the feature and the surviving sentence carries the claim.
when: Feature showcases where a screenshot or image can demonstrate the point.
fails: Features that are conceptual, technical, or invisible in a screenshot still need the copy.

claim: For a closing CTA, set heavy bold type left-aligned over a full-bleed image rather than centred over flat colour.
why: Left alignment gives the type a reading edge and weight; the image keeps the emotional register of the rest of the page instead of dropping into a generic coloured band.
when: Final conversion sections on image-led marketing pages.

claim: Strip decorative dividing lines and eyebrow labels from borrowed testimonial layouts to break up blocky, over-compartmentalised grids.
why: Rules and labels add visual weight without adding information, making the section read as boxes rather than voices.
when: Testimonial or card-grid sections that feel heavy or rigid.

claim: When a reference's how-it-works section reads as numbered steps, remove the step framing but keep the sequence — let scale and imagery carry the progression.
why: Explicit step chrome makes a product feel procedural and effortful; the same order communicated through visuals feels like a narrative instead.
when: Explaining a product flow that isn't literally a checklist the user must complete.
fails: Genuinely sequential onboarding or setup, where numbered steps are the clearest form.

claim: If you generate sections from a component library, source them all from one library so they share the same spacing, type and colour primitives.
why: Shared primitives produce cross-page consistency that is hard to maintain when each section is authored from scratch.
when: Assembling pages quickly from prebuilt or AI-generated blocks.
fails: Stated inside a sponsor read, so treat it as vendor framing rather than a neutral finding — the underlying consistency point still holds for any single design system.

claim: When auditing a design, score it on two separate axes — is it correct (usable, legible, on-spec) and is it memorable (has a point of view a user could describe afterwards) — and treat a high-correctness, low-memorability result as a real defect to fix, not a finished design.
why: Conventional critique only catches errors, so a layout that violates no rules passes review even when it is indistinguishable from every competitor; without a second axis there is no mechanism that ever flags blandness.
when: Reviewing marketing sites, landing pages, or brand surfaces where differentiation and emotional response are part of the job.
fails: Utility-first contexts — dashboards, admin tools, checkout, high-frequency task UI — where familiarity and predictability beat personality, and 'unmemorable' is the correct outcome.

claim: Audit a site and name each specific failure before designing anything; treat the diagnosis as a separate pass from the redesign.
why: A redesign that starts from taste produces a different-looking site with the same structural problems; naming defects first gives each design decision something to answer to.
when: Redesigning or overhauling an existing product or marketing site.
fails: Greenfield work with no artifact to critique, or when the audit becomes a stalling device instead of a short pass.

claim: Judge a landing page by whether it says anything, not just whether it looks clean; a page with no content to evaluate is failing even when nothing on it is technically wrong.
why: Emptiness reads as minimalism to the designer and as an absent value proposition to the visitor — 'no errors' is not the same as 'communicates'.
when: Homepages and top-of-funnel pages that must establish what the product is.
fails: Deliberate single-purpose splash or holding pages where one action is the entire job.

claim: Don't pin decorative elements — rotated text, ornamental labels, persistent flourishes — to the viewport during scroll; let them scroll away with their section.
why: A fixed element re-enters peripheral vision on every scroll frame and keeps drawing attention it never repays with information.
when: Decorative or purely stylistic elements. Genuinely functional persistent UI (nav, cart, progress) is a different case.
fails: The sticky element carries navigation or state the user needs continuously.

claim: Whitespace is a finite budget — increasing it past the point where elements stop reading as a group produces disjointedness, not elegance.
why: Space is only meaningful in contrast; when everything is equally far from everything else, no grouping signal survives and each element floats alone.
when: Editorial and marketing layouts using generous spacing as a style.
fails: Genuinely dense interfaces, where the usual failure runs the other direction.

claim: Scale display type and surrounding whitespace together; oversized headlines inside already-loose layouts compound into fragmentation.
why: Both large type and wide gaps push content apart — applying them at once means no two elements ever sit close enough to relate.
when: Hero and feature sections built around large type.
fails: Full-bleed typographic posters where isolation of a single statement is the intent.

claim: Create hierarchy by moving related elements closer together before reaching for size, weight, or colour changes.
why: Proximity alone tells the eye what belongs to what, and costs nothing in the type or colour system.
when: Any layout where elements read as unrelated fragments.
fails: Elements that genuinely are peers with no grouping to express; tightening then just creates false relationships.

claim: Keep one type scale across a page; if a lower section drops to noticeably smaller text, treat that as evidence of two designs stitched together.
why: An abrupt scale shift mid-page reads as a seam, and the visitor stops trusting that the sections belong to one product.
when: Long-scroll pages where spec, detail, or secondary content follows a marketing hero.
fails: Deliberate, systematic scale steps — captions, footnotes, footers — that repeat consistently and read as part of one scale.

claim: When a section only breaks stylistically because its content doesn't fit the page's model, fix the information architecture before restyling it.
why: Restyling mismatched content just hides the mismatch; the reason the section needed different treatment is that it was never structured to belong.
when: Dense secondary content — spec tables, comparisons, technical detail — bolted onto a narrative page.
fails: The break really is cosmetic and a style pass resolves it, in which case IA work is overkill.

claim: Treat page length as a design defect in its own right — cut a page to the length its content actually needs rather than padding to fill a scroll.
why: Length inflated by spacing rather than substance dilutes every section and makes the page feel emptier the longer it gets.
when: Marketing and product pages built as long scrolls.
fails: Genuinely deep content — documentation, long-form editorial — where length reflects real substance.

claim: Set cohesion as the explicit success criterion for a redesign: one type scale, one spacing rhythm, one structural logic top to bottom.
why: The listed defects — emptiness, loose spacing, type-scale breaks, IA mismatch, bloated length — are all symptoms of a page assembled section by section without a shared system.
when: Full-site overhauls where individual patches would leave the seams visible.
fails: Targeted fixes with a limited mandate, where a systemic rewrite exceeds scope.

claim: Judge a UI at two zoom levels before accepting it: the whole-canvas first impression, then each card, label and data point read on its own — treat any component that stops making sense in isolation as a defect, regardless of how good the composition looks.
why: Portfolio-shot aesthetics are optimised for a thumbnail-scale glance; the visual polish (spacing rhythm, colour harmony, imagery) can carry a layout whose individual elements convey nothing usable, so a single-zoom review systematically misses functional failures.
when: Reviewing or drawing inspiration from decorative concept work, and when self-critiquing your own dashboard or data-dense layout before publishing.
fails: Not addressed in this chapter; the criteria for what makes a component 'not make sense' are deferred to later chapters.

claim: When an existing design fails at the component level rather than the surface level, rebuild it from an empty canvas instead of patching the visible symptoms.
why: The presenter frames the problem as structural — the whole design, not just the chart card he had previously lifted — so a from-scratch pass is presented as the way to arrive at a defensible layout.
when: The source artefact's underlying information structure is what's wrong, not its styling.
fails: Not addressed; no cost/benefit given for redesign versus targeted fixes on shipped production work.

claim: Do not repeat a single section layout (e.g. text-left/image-right) down an entire page; vary the section structure — full-bleed, stacked, multi-column, offset — so the page has rhythm.
why: An unbroken repeating pattern gives the eye no reason to continue; variation creates momentum that carries the scroll.
when: Long-scroll marketing and landing pages with three or more content sections.
fails: Alternating rows are still legitimate as one ingredient among several, and dense documentation or comparison pages may want deliberate uniformity for scannability.

claim: Replace generic stock photography with visuals of the actual product — UI screenshots, interface details, or purpose-made illustration of the thing being sold.
why: Stock imagery that has no relationship to the product signals that no decision was made, and it fails to explain or sell what the product does.
when: Any product landing page, especially software where the interface is the product.

claim: Keep corner radius consistent across the page: if buttons are rounded, apply a matching radius scale to images, cards, and containers rather than mixing sharp-cornered media with rounded controls.
why: Inconsistent shape language reads as accidental and breaks the sense that the page is one designed system.
when: Any interface mixing media, surfaces, and controls.
fails: A deliberately mixed shape language can work when the contrast is systematic (e.g. all media square, all controls pill) rather than incidental.

claim: Using one typeface family throughout is the correct baseline; earn differentiation through weight, size, and spacing rather than by adding fonts.
why: A single family already gives a coherent foundation; hierarchy problems at this level come from undifferentiated scale and loose spacing, not from a lack of typefaces.
when: Landing pages and product marketing sites at any level of polish.
fails: Not addressed — a considered display/body pairing is a normal step at higher levels.

claim: Widen the gap between heading and body: increase the size and weight jump, and tighten heading letter-spacing and line-height so the hierarchy is unmistakable at a glance.
why: When every text block reads at similar visual weight, nothing directs the eye and the reader has to do the ranking work themselves.
when: Hero sections and section headers where a scanner should absorb the point in under a second.

claim: Cut body copy to the shortest statement that carries the point; never ship a paragraph-length block in a hero or feature section.
why: Visitors scan rather than read, so a wall of text is skipped entirely and the message is lost.
when: Above-the-fold and feature sections on conversion-focused pages.
fails: Deeper pages — docs, pricing detail, technical explanation — legitimately need prose.

claim: Remove copy that repeats information already visible on screen, such as naming the company in a headline when the logo sits directly above it.
why: Redundant words consume the reader's limited attention without adding anything.
when: Hero headlines, nav-adjacent copy, and any text sitting near a logo or label that states the same thing.

claim: Give the nav bar internal hierarchy: style the primary action (sign up) as a filled button, elevate the one or two links that matter most, and de-emphasise the rest with lighter weight or muted colour.
why: A menu where every item looks identical fails to point at the action you want taken, so the most valuable click is buried among housekeeping links.
when: Any site navigation containing a conversion action.

claim: Balance the nav across the header rather than stacking everything on the right — for example logo left, links centred, primary action right.
why: Weighting all elements to one side leaves visual dead space and makes the top of the page feel lopsided.
when: Horizontal top navigation bars on desktop widths.
fails: Minimal nav bars with only a logo and one action can sit at the outer edges without imbalance.

claim: Apply the accent colour selectively to the elements you want noticed, instead of every element that technically accepts it.
why: When a brand colour is used everywhere it stops signalling importance and starts competing with the text it sits beside.
when: Pages with a single strong brand accent colour.

claim: Build a working colour palette in the interface itself — surfaces, text tiers, borders, accent — rather than letting the photography supply the page's colour.
why: Leaning on imagery to carry colour means the palette shifts with every asset and the page never establishes its own identity.
when: Landing pages where colour has not been deliberately specified.

claim: Treat default hover states as the absence of motion, not as motion design; add intentional entrance, scroll, or state transitions to make the page feel alive.
why: A link changing colour on hover is browser behaviour; it contributes nothing to how considered or responsive the product feels.
when: Marketing pages aiming to feel premium or crafted.

claim: Audit a page as a set of separate disciplines — layout, imagery, shape language, typography, copy, navigation, colour, motion — and grade each one, rather than judging the page as a single impression.
why: 'It works but it's not good' is not actionable; splitting the page into named axes turns a vague feeling into a specific ordered list of fixes.
when: Critiquing or improving an existing design, your own or a client's.

claim: Treat a page that functions correctly but reflects no decisions as failing, not as passing — functional correctness is the floor, not the goal.
why: The distance between a template and a converting page is entirely in the decisions made on top of a working baseline.
when: Evaluating commercial pages whose purpose is conversion.
fails: Internal tools, MVPs, and throwaway prototypes where speed genuinely outranks craft.

claim: Identify the two or three parts of the craft you are reliably bad at, and permanently assign each one a dedicated tool instead of re-attempting it by hand every project.
why: Skill gaps that recur every project are a fixed tax on delivery speed; a tool converts a recurring struggle into a one-click step and frees attention for the parts you are actually good at.
when: Solo designers or small teams shipping repeatedly, where the same weak spot (logo marks, type pairing, gradients, motion) blocks progress each time.
fails: For a discipline central to the engagement — never outsource brand identity work to a generator on a branding project — and when it becomes a way to avoid ever building the skill.

claim: When a layout reads as flat grey boxes, fix it by dropping in a pre-built interactive component (button, toggle, loader) from a component library rather than by adjusting spacing and colour further.
why: A grey wireframe usually lacks interaction affordance and detail, not measurements; a finished component injects both at once.
when: Mid-fidelity Figma work that has correct structure but no visual life yet.
fails: If borrowed components come from mismatched visual systems, the file gains detail but loses coherence — restyle them to one radius, stroke and colour scale before shipping.

claim: Prefer asset sources that support direct paste-into-Figma over ones that only export code or flat images.
why: Every format conversion is a manual step and a chance to lose editability; layered vector paste keeps the asset adjustable in place.
when: Sourcing components, icons or illustrations mid-design.
fails: When the asset's value is its runtime behaviour (CSS animation, WebGL) — that has to be handed to engineering as code, not as a static frame.

claim: Generate font pairings with a pairing engine, then judge the result by eye and regenerate, instead of choosing two typefaces from first principles.
why: Pairing is a similarity/contrast problem that a tool trained across a large font corpus solves faster than an untrained intuition; you keep the veto, not the search.
when: Early type exploration, or any project without an inherited brand typeface.
fails: When brand guidelines already specify type, or when the pairing must carry specific meaning or language support the generator does not model.

claim: Use placeholder logo marks in comps so that an unresolved brand identity never blocks layout, spacing and hierarchy decisions.
why: A missing logo stalls the whole composition; a neutral stand-in of roughly correct weight and width lets you evaluate everything around it.
when: Client work or personal projects where the mark is undecided or out of scope.
fails: If the placeholder survives into anything client-facing without being flagged as temporary, or if it is treated as the final identity.

claim: For UI motion, pick an animation tool whose editor mirrors your static design tool rather than a full motion-graphics package.
why: The dominant cost of animating is relearning an unfamiliar timeline and object model; a familiar canvas removes it, and UI motion rarely needs the depth of a compositor.
when: Prototyping short interface transitions, hover states, and micro-animations.
fails: Broadcast-grade work, complex compositing, effects, or long-form sequences still need the heavier tool.

claim: Build mesh and multi-stop gradients in a dedicated gradient generator and bring the export back in, rather than approximating them with stacked layers in Figma.
why: Vector design tools do not model true mesh interpolation, so hand-built approximations cost far more time and still band or look flat.
when: Backgrounds, hero sections and any surface needing soft multi-directional colour blends.
fails: The export is a raster — it will not respond to theme changes, needs resolution planning for large surfaces, and adds file weight.

claim: Break inspiration hunting down to the section level: search 'pricing section' or 'testimonial section' in a section-indexed library instead of browsing whole-page showcases.
why: You are almost never stuck on an entire page — you are stuck on one block, and full-page galleries force you to mentally extract it every time.
when: A single region of a page resists resolution while the rest of the layout is settled.
fails: Assembling a page from unrelated best-in-class sections produces a patchwork with no rhythm; the sections still have to be reconciled to one grid and type scale.

claim: Choose icon sets that expose parameters — corner radius, stroke weight, style — and set those to match your existing UI rather than accepting the set's defaults.
why: Icons read as foreign the moment their stroke weight or corner treatment disagrees with the surrounding components; parametric sets let you match instead of compromise.
when: Adding an icon family to an interface that already has a defined radius and stroke language.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Collect candidate icons or assets into a single staging folder and review them together as a set before exporting any of them.
why: Icons chosen one at a time drift in weight, optical size and metaphor; seeing them side by side surfaces the mismatch while it is still cheap to fix.
when: Any time more than two or three icons will appear in the same view.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Keep a curated reference library of real shipped micro-interactions from mature products, and consult it before inventing an interaction from scratch.
why: Large product teams have already tested these behaviours at scale, so they encode solved problems in feedback, timing and delight rather than untested ideas.
when: Designing hover states, transitions, empty states, and confirmation feedback.
fails: Copying a heavily branded interaction into a product with a different tone, or adding motion to interactions where speed matters more than delight.

claim: Maintain several stock photo sources and judge them by findability, not catalogue size — a smaller, well-organised library often beats a huge one.
why: Search time dominates image sourcing; a tightly curated and categorised set converges on a usable image faster than an enormous unstructured one.
when: Sourcing photography for marketing pages and content sections.
fails: Highly specific subject matter still requires the largest catalogue available, or commissioned photography.

claim: Deliberately source from less-known libraries rather than the two or three defaults everyone uses.
why: Ubiquitous stock and asset sources produce work that looks like everyone else's; obscurity is a cheap source of freshness.
when: Any project where visual differentiation matters.
fails: Obscure sources may have unclear or restrictive licensing — verify usage rights before commercial use.

claim: Start large multi-page projects from a comprehensive community Figma kit of pre-built sections and elements rather than from an empty file.
why: A kit with dozens of pages of sections supplies both a component inventory and a set of layout precedents, so early work becomes selection and adaptation instead of construction.
when: Marketing sites and landing pages under time pressure.
fails: Kit-derived pages default to generic; every section needs re-typing, re-colouring and often re-structuring to carry a distinct brand.

claim: Treat recurring small graphic elements like arrows and connectors as an asset library problem, not a drawing problem.
why: Vector pen tools are slow and inconsistent for hand-drawn accents; a variety pack gives consistent, reusable options instantly.
when: Annotations, presentation slides, callouts, and hand-drawn accents in marketing layouts.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: When benchmarking your portfolio, use showcases that state each designer's years of experience, location and work type, and compare only against a comparable band.
why: Context-free comparison against fifteen-year veterans produces demoralisation rather than useful signal; matched-experience comparison yields an achievable target.
when: Portfolio review, self-assessment, and setting improvement goals.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: Use the tool's own website as evidence of its quality — a resource site with a well-executed hover state or transition is usually made by people worth learning from.
why: Craft in a site's own interactions signals the same care in its output; the presenter repeatedly stops to admire and dissect these.
when: Evaluating unfamiliar resources, and hunting for interaction patterns to reverse-engineer.
fails: A polished marketing site can mask a thin or abandoned product — check the actual asset depth too.

claim: Build baseline literacy in AI-product UX patterns now, on the assumption most interfaces will soon have an AI-adjacent surface.
why: AI features behave unpredictably — impressive in some cases, wrong in others — so their interfaces need patterns for uncertainty, correction and trust that conventional UI training does not cover.
when: Designers positioning for near-term product work.
fails: Not addressed.

claim: When the same change needs to land on many instances of a repeated element, select all instances and edit them in one pass rather than repeating the edit frame by frame.
why: Repeating an identical edit across frames is slow and drifts — some frames get missed or edited slightly differently, so the file stops being a reliable source of truth.
when: A design has repeated structures across multiple frames, screens, or states and a change applies uniformly to all of them.
fails: The instances are only superficially similar and actually need to diverge — bulk editing then erases intentional differences.

claim: Name layers with a consistent scheme and keep repeated groups in the same relative position inside their parents, so automated 'select all matching layers' can find them.
why: The matching engine identifies siblings by layer name and by position within the grouping hierarchy; inconsistent names or ad-hoc nesting make the match fail and force manual selection.
when: Building repeated components, screen variants, or any structure you expect to edit in bulk later.
fails: Generic auto-names like 'Frame 42' or 'Group 7' repeat across unrelated elements — matching then over-selects things you did not intend to change.

claim: Before running a bulk edit, wrap the frames you intend to affect in a section and select from there, so the operation cannot reach frames outside it.
why: Automatic matching is greedy by design; an explicit container turns an unbounded selection into a bounded one and makes the blast radius visible before you commit.
when: A canvas holds many similar frames but only a subset — one flow, one platform, one variant set — should receive the change.
fails: The frames you want are scattered across sections; forcing them into one section for a single edit reorganises the file for a temporary need.

claim: Apply auto layout to several separate frames in one action (select them all, then Shift+A) instead of converting each frame individually.
why: Layout structure is the kind of change that must be identical across a set to behave predictably; applying it in one action guarantees the set shares the same structural treatment.
when: Retrofitting auto layout onto a set of frames that were built loosely, or standardising an existing screen set.
fails: The frames have genuinely different internal arrangements — one blanket auto layout direction will fight some of them.

claim: To reposition an element consistently across many auto layouts, move it once with all copies selected and let the change propagate, rather than nudging each copy.
why: Manual per-copy nudging accumulates sub-pixel and ordering inconsistencies that auto layout would otherwise have enforced for free.
when: Reordering or relocating a shared element — an icon, a label, a button — inside a repeated layout pattern.

claim: Treat bulk text replacement across many objects as a single operation: multi-select the text layers, then type the new content once.
why: Content changes to repeated labels are high-volume and low-judgement; doing them one at a time is where typos and stale strings enter a file.
when: Updating shared copy — nav labels, CTA text, placeholder strings — that appears in identical form across frames.
fails: Each instance carries different real content and only looks repetitive; a single typed value would flatten meaningful copy variation.

claim: Begin a redesign by identifying specific weaknesses in comparable product pages, then define a clear target page to improve.
why: Concrete critique creates a reasoned design brief instead of treating the redesign as purely decorative.
when: Starting a landing-page or brand refresh project.

claim: Build an AI-product visual language by combining soft mesh gradients, subtle noise texture, and generously rounded components.
why: These cues are presented as a coherent visual shorthand for contemporary AI interfaces.
when: Creating a polished, approachable marketing page for an AI product.
fails: When the product needs a deliberately utilitarian, restrained, or non-trend-driven visual identity.

claim: Use adjacent products and existing brand surfaces as references before establishing the redesign direction.
why: References help the new page feel competitive while remaining connected to the wider product ecosystem.
when: Redesigning a product page within an established company or category.

claim: Create low-fidelity wireframes before high-fidelity screens so you can generate and compare layout ideas rapidly.
why: Rough representations reduce the cost of exploration and help identify a stronger layout before visual-detail work begins.
when: Planning the structure, hierarchy, navigation, or task flow of a digital product.

claim: Include selected rough sketches and early wireframes in a case study to show how the final solution emerged.
why: Process artifacts help readers understand the decisions and iteration behind the outcome.
when: Presenting a UX process or portfolio case study.
fails: When the artifacts do not clarify a decision, task, or design change and only add noise.

claim: Keep early wireframes deliberately rough; use simple shading, arrows, and notes instead of polishing their appearance.
why: The wireframe’s purpose is to communicate and evaluate structure, not to simulate a finished interface.
when: Exploring or explaining preliminary layouts.

claim: Test wireframes with a few people before building a complete prototype, then revise and test again.
why: Early observation reveals whether proposed interactions and information flow are intuitive while changes remain inexpensive.
when: You have a proposed flow or layout whose usability assumptions need validation.

claim: Connect research findings to the wireframes that they informed or changed.
why: Making the relationship visible demonstrates evidence-based iteration rather than unsupported design choices.
when: Documenting testing and iteration in a case study.

claim: Do not treat adherence to baseline layout, navigation, and spacing conventions as sufficient; add intentional visual interest when the site needs to capture attention.
why: A design can be usable and polished while still feeling generic or forgettable.
when: Designing marketing, portfolio, editorial, or other attention-driven experiences where differentiation matters.
fails: A business specifically needs a straightforward, low-distraction interface and the added expression would hinder its goals.

claim: Evaluate a screen against a concrete item or answer the user is trying to find.
why: People often search for a particular file or setting rather than consuming an entire interface.
when: Reviewing a task-oriented interface.
fails: Linear reading experiences may require sustained comprehension instead of rapid lookup.

claim: Judge alignment, grouping and visual substitutions by whether they reduce search effort.
why: These devices support locating information, not merely surface polish.
when: Comparing interface revisions.
fails: Faster recognition alone does not establish that a task is correctly understood.
